Ternary Partitioning of Continental-Scale Water Clarity Bio-Optical Modeling and Ternary Diagnostics Across U.S. Streams, Lakes, and Estuaries (1970–2025) James W. Jawitz, Matthew J. Cohen, and Matthew R.V. Ross October 21, 2026 Overview Water clarity is one of our oldest and most intuitive lenses into aquatic ecosystems. For more than a century, hydrologists and limnologists have lowered Secchi disks into rivers, lakes, and estuaries to measure how deeply light penetrates the water column. Yet Secchi disk depth (\(z_{SD}\), in meters) alone tells us only how much light is lost—not what is blocking it. Across inland and coastal waters, diffuse light attenuation (\(k_d = 1 / z_{SD}\); Lee et al. 2015) is governed by pure water (\(k_w\)) and three primary light-attenuating constituents (LACs): non-algal particles (NAP), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and phytoplankton chlorophyll a (\(\text{Chl }a\)). Under the additive Beer–Lambert model, Secchi depth can be written directly in terms of constituent concentrations: \[z_{SD} = \frac{1}{k_w + \alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{NAP} + \alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC} + \alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\,\text{Chl }a}\] To understand how these three constituents partition water clarity across the contiguous United States, we built an open-source pipeline on top of the AquaMatch data suite (Brousil et al. 2024a, 2024b, 2025; De La Torre et al. 2025)—the successor to AquaSat (Ross et al. 2019). Combining 274,445 simultaneous four-variable matchups (Secchi + Chl a + DOC + TSS/SSC) for model calibration with 479,666 three-constituent matchups across 39,423 monitoring stations (1970–2025), we estimate regional specific attenuation coefficients (\(\alpha_i\)) across U.S. EPA Level III ecoregions and project nearly half a million water quality observations into ternary attenuation space. Why Optical Partitioning & Total Visibility Both Matter ({sonicray} 3D Simulation) Ternary diagrams are a powerful way to visualize which constituent dominates light attenuation (\(f_{\text{NAP}} + f_{\text{DOC}} + f_{\text{Chl }a} = 1\)), but proportions alone miss a critical physical dimension: total visibility (\(z_{SD}\)). Two lakes sitting at the exact same coordinate in ternary space can represent either a crystal-clear oligotrophic basin (\(z_{SD} > 5\text{ m}\)) or a murky waterbody (\(z_{SD} < 0.4\text{ m}\)) when total constituent concentrations scale up. Moreover, each constituent alters the underwater light field in a distinct way: Chlorophyll a (Algae): Absorbs blue and red light while cells scatter green wavelengths, shifting water from deep blue to emerald green. DOC (Brownification): Absorbs short wavelengths exponentially with negligible particulate scattering, turning water into dark tea-stained blackwater. NAP / TSS (Sediment): Strongly backscatters broadband light, turning water chalky tan/ochre and driving the steepest collapse in Secchi visibility. Section 2 Simultaneous Matchups & Initial Hygiene (prep.R) To partition light attenuation among phytoplankton, non-algal particles, and dissolved organic carbon, we need field samples where chl_a, doc, and tss were collected on the same day at the same station (MonitoringLocationIdentifier and date)—which we refer to as matchups. Calibrating our bio-optical model additionally requires a same-day Secchi disk depth (secchi) measurement. am <- get_aquamatch() # 490,209 joined 3-LAC records (1970–2025) simul <- build_simultaneous(am, require_secchi = TRUE) no_secchi <- build_simultaneous(am, require_secchi = FALSE) 2.1 Four Initial Hygiene Filters Before statistical screening, build_simultaneous() in R/prep.R applies four simple, deterministic hygiene rules: Ambient water bodies only: Excludes industrial/municipal Facility outflows, retaining Estuary, Lake, and Stream sites. True Secchi measurements (for 4-variable calibration): Requires sdd_approx == 0 (excluding turbidity tubes) and sdd_mdl <= 1 (excluding \(\le 0.01\text{ m}\) floor placeholders). Gross unit-error caps: Removes obvious \(1{,}000\times\) reporting-unit mixups (\(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\) reported as \(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)): \(0 < z_{SD} < 15\text{ m}\), \(\text{Chl }a < 1000\ \mu\text{g L}^{-1}\), \(\text{TSS} < 1000\text{ mg L}^{-1}\), and \(\text{DOC} < 50\text{ mg L}^{-1}\). Same-day deduplication: Collapses duplicate agency uploads of the same bottle sample (distinct(SiteID, date, secchi, chl_a, doc, tss)). Section 3 Separating Non-Algal Particles (NAP) from Bulk TSS Our additive Beer–Lambert model partitions non-water light attenuation among three mutually exclusive pools: phytoplankton (Chl a), non-algal suspended particles (NAP: mineral sediment and detritus), and dissolved organic matter (DOC). Because standard gravimetric filtration measures bulk Total Suspended Solids (TSS)—which captures both mineral sediment and living algal cells on the filter—we subtract living phytoplankton dry mass from bulk TSS before fitting the model: Optical Component Field Measurement Model Predictor & Units Phytoplankton (\(\alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\,\text{Chl }a\)) Chlorophyll a (\(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{Chl }a\) (\(\text{mg m}^{-3} = \mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) used directly Non-algal particles (\(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{NAP}\)) Bulk TSS / SSC (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{NAP} = \text{TSS} - \text{biomass}(\text{Chl }a)\) (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) Dissolved organic matter (\(\alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC}\)) DOC (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{DOC}\) (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) used directly Following Gohin et al. (2005), we estimate phytoplankton dry biomass (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) from \(\text{Chl }a\) (\(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) as a power law that accounts for intracellular photoacclimation (lower carbon-to-chlorophyll ratios in nutrient-rich blooms; Geider et al. 1997; Cloern et al. 1995): \[\text{biomass}_{\text{algal}}\ [\text{mg L}^{-1}] = 0.234\,(\text{Chl }a)^{0.57}, \qquad \text{NAP} = \text{TSS} - 0.234\,(\text{Chl }a)^{0.57}\] Figure 3.1: (a) Empirical TSS vs. Chl a across matchups overlaid with the nonlinear Gohin et al. (2005) algal biomass curve (solid black) and constant linear dry-mass:Chl a ratios (dashed). Section 4 Analytical Floors & Beer–Lambert Plausibility Screening 4.1 Stage 1: Analytical Reporting Floors (trim_simultaneous()) 4.2 Stage 2: Beer–Lambert Residual Screen (\(\pm 2.5\text{ SD} \approx 5\text{-fold}\)) & “Odd-One-Out” Rule 4.3 Pure-Water Attenuation Offset (\(k_w\)) and \(k_d\) Distributions

Section 4 Analytical Floors & Beer–Lambert Plausibility Screening Even after parameter and unit harmonization, roughly 2% of multi-agency WQP records contain field-recording or unit-entry anomalies that can heavily leverage ordinary least squares (OLS) slopes. However, simple marginal quantile trimming (clipping the top and bottom 0.1% or 1% of each variable independently) throws away genuine oligotrophic alpine lakes (Secchi up to 13.96 m) and real storm-flow sediment plumes (TSS up to 978 mg/L) while missing joint physical contradictions in the middle of the distribution. To clean recording errors without truncating real extremes or introducing statistical circularity, R/prep.R uses a two-stage protocol (n = 274,445): 4.1 Stage 1: Analytical Reporting Floors (trim_simultaneous()) Rather than dropping low-concentration tails, entries reported below standard EPA/USGS Method Detection Limits (MDLs) are floored via ifelse(x < floor, floor, x) (chl_a = 0.10 µg/L, doc = 0.25 mg/L, tss = 0.50 mg/L, secchi = 0.01 m), retaining 100% of the 281,439 simultaneous 4-variable matchups: Variable Analytical Floor (MDL) Median 99.9th Percentile Maximum Retained Chlorophyll a (µg/L) 0.10 7.33 323.000 990.290 Dissolved Organic Carbon (mg/L) 0.25 6.20 48.000 49.985 Total Suspended Solids / SSC (mg/L) 0.50 8.50 340.000 978.000 Secchi Disk Depth (m) 0.01 0.80 7.687 14.330 4.2 Stage 2: Beer–Lambert Residual Screen (\(\pm 2.5\text{ SD} \approx 5\text{-fold}\)) & “Odd-One-Out” Rule When all four measurements (Secchi, Chl a, DOC, and TSS) are collected on the same water sample, they provide an internal physical cross-check: do the three water-chemistry constituents agree with the observed Secchi depth in Beer–Lambert space, or is one of the four measurements an obvious outlier? To evaluate physical agreement a priori—without using any fitted regression parameters from our data—we compare observed diffuse attenuation (\(k_d = 1 / z_{SD}\)) against canonical Beer–Lambert attenuation (\(k_{d,\text{lit}}\)) computed from published optical cross-sections (Kirk 1994; Morris et al. 1995; Bannister 1974; Gohin et al. 2005): \[k_{d,\text{lit}} = 0.080 + 0.040\,\max(0, \text{NAP}) + 0.070\,\text{DOC} + 0.016\,\text{Chl }a, \qquad r = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{k_d}{k_{d,\text{lit}}}\right)\] Across all 281,439 four-variable matchups, the log residual \(r\) is centered at virtually zero (\(\bar{r} = 0.013\), confirming that literature cross-sections match the continental median without bias) with a standard deviation of \(\text{SD}(r) = 0.270\text{ log}_{10}\text{ units}\). Standardizing each sample’s residual as \(z_r = (r - \bar{r}) / \text{SD}(r)\), we require \(|z_r| \le 2.5\text{ SD}\) (|r - r_bar| <= 0.674, a 4.7-fold [\(\sim 5\times\)] tolerance). This retains 274,445 (97.51%) training observations and flags 6,994 (2.49%) discordant outliers, which fall into two distinct physical categories with asymmetric disposition (Figure 4.1a): Upper Tail (\(z_r > +2.5\text{ SD}\), 5,177 records = 1.84%) — Secchi is the odd one out (shallow streambed bottom hits): Field crews lower a Secchi disk in a clear, shallow stream (\(0.05\text{–}0.20\text{ m}\) deep) where the disk rests on the gravel streambed while still visible, and record the water depth as the Secchi depth (Secchi = 0.05–0.20 m, implying \(k_d = 5\text{–}20\text{ m}^{-1}\)) even though Chl a, DOC, and TSS are all low and mutually consistent (\(\text{TSS} < 3\text{ mg L}^{-1}\), \(\text{DOC} < 3\text{ mg L}^{-1}\)). Because Secchi is censored by the streambed while the three water-chemistry measurements are valid, these records are excluded from regression training (build_training()), but in the ternary application dataset (build_application()) only Secchi is set to NA—rescuing the valid 3-constituent water chemistry with a modeled Secchi depth! Lower Tail (\(z_r < -2.5\text{ SD}\), 1,817 records = 0.65%) — One of the chemistry constituents (Chl a, DOC, or TSS) is the odd one out: A clear Secchi reading (2–10 m) is paired with two low chemistry measurements and one extreme chemistry spike (\(\text{Chl }a > 500\ \mu\text{g L}^{-1}\) or \(\text{TSS} > 200\text{ mg L}^{-1}\)), typically caused by a \(1{,}000\times\) unit conversion error (\(\text{ng L}^{-1}\) entered as \(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) or bottle mismatch. Because all three constituents are required to place a sample in ternary space, lower-tail records are excluded from both training and ternary application. Section 5 Hierarchical Ecoregion Stratification (ecoregions.R) A gram of dissolved organic carbon or suspended sediment does not attenuate the exact same amount of light everywhere. Humic DOC drained from northern peatlands is darker and more aromatic than autochthonous DOC in arid reservoirs (Spencer et al. 2012; Griffin et al. 2018), and fine clay suspensions scatter light much more efficiently per unit mass than coarse glacial silt (Bowers et al. 2020). To capture this regional biogeochemical coherence across streams, lakes, and estuaries within a single continental framework, eco_join() in R/ecoregions.R assigns each monitoring station (SiteID) to its nested U.S. EPA / CEC North American Ecoregion across Levels I–IV (Omernik & Griffith 2014). Nearshore estuarine stations located slightly seaward of coastline polygons are matched to the nearest coastal ecoregion via sf::st_nearest_feature(), guaranteeing a strict 1-to-1 mapping from SiteID to ecoregion. Section 7 Coefficient Stability & Sample-Size Convergence (Fig. S1) Do regional differences in fitted attenuation slopes (\(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}, \alpha_{\text{DOC}}, \alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\)) reflect real biogeochemical differences across ecoregions, or just small-sample estimation noise? To answer this, we randomly partition the 274,445 training matchups into \(G\) subsets of varying sample size (\(n/50, n/100, \dots, n/10{,}000\), plus \(G=1\)) and refit the three-constituent model across 10 independent Monte Carlo replicates (random_subset_coefs() in R/models.R, seed P$random_seed = 20240826). Figure 7.1: Figure S1: Coefficient coherence cones across sample sizes. Grey ribbons span the 0.001%–99.999% quantiles of slopes fitted to random subsets of size n across all data and by water-body type. Colored circles mark Level III ecoregion fits (Models 7 and 8). Once group sample size exceeds \(n \approx 1{,}000\), random sampling variability narrows into a tight cone around the continental mean (grey ribbon). Regional estimates of \(\alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\) (chl_a, top row) stay tightly clustered inside the random-sampling cone, whereas ecoregion-specific slopes for \(\alpha_{\text{DOC}}\) (doc, middle row) and \(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}\) (tss_dead, bottom row) spread well outside the random-sampling envelope even at \(n > 10{,}000\). That spread reflects genuine regional differences in dissolved organic matter aromaticity (Spencer et al. 2012; Griffin et al. 2018) and suspended particle size and mineralogy (Dodds & Whiles 2004; Gohin et al. 2005). Section 8 Continental Application & Dominance Regimes (apply_model7()) 8.1 Continental 3-Constituent Application Dataset (n = 479,666) Once Model 7 is calibrated on the 274,445 four-variable training matchups, it requires only the three constituent concentrations (\(\text{NAP}\), \(\text{DOC}\), and \(\text{Chl }a\)) to partition non-water light attenuation. Under our asymmetric “odd-one-out” rule (Rule 2), when a shallow stream sample has a streambed bottom-hit Secchi reading (\(z_r > +2.5\text{ SD}\), 5,177 training records) alongside low, mutually consistent water chemistry (Chl a, DOC, and TSS), only the secchi field is set to NA so the valid 3-constituent chemistry is retained with a modeled Secchi depth. Conversely, lower-tail chemistry unit errors (\(z_r < -2.5\text{ SD}\), 1,817 records) are dropped.
